titlePl: Matura PR: Zdrowie — 180 haseł do gier LingoSpark
titleEn: Matura Extended: Health — 180 terms for LingoSpark games
blurbPl: Dział Zdrowie na maturę rozszerzoną: system ochrony zdrowia, choroby, uzależnienia i profilaktyka. Fiszki ENG–PL.
blurbEn: Extended-level Matura Health vocabulary: the healthcare system, illness, addiction and prevention. ENG–PL flashcards for LingoSpark games.

items.definitionEn: a state of being healthy, comfortable and content, not only free from illness
items.example: Regular sleep and close friendships support mental well-being.

items.definitionEn: how good or bad a person’s life feels in health, comfort and opportunity
items.example: Pain can reduce quality of life even when tests look normal.

items.definitionEn: the average number of years a person in a group is expected to live
items.example: Life expectancy has risen, but not equally in every region.

items.definitionEn: organised efforts to protect and improve the health of a whole population
items.example: Public health campaigns reduced smoking among teenagers.

items.definitionEn: the ability to find, understand and use information to make health decisions
items.example: Low health literacy makes prescription labels harder to follow.

items.definitionEn: unfair differences in health between social or economic groups
items.example: Health inequality is wider in areas with poor housing and low income.

items.definitionEn: medical services that stop illness before it starts or catches it early
items.example: Preventive care includes vaccinations and regular blood-pressure checks.

items.definitionEn: something that raises the chance of developing a disease
items.example: Smoking is a major risk factor for heart disease.

items.definitionEn: an existing long-term illness that makes other problems more serious
items.example: People with an underlying condition were offered the vaccine first.

items.definitionEn: the body’s defences against infection
items.example: Stress and poor sleep can weaken the immune system.

items.definitionEn: activity that encourages people to live in ways that protect their health
items.example: The city funded health promotion in schools and workplaces.

items.definitionEn: organised tests offered to a group to find disease early
items.example: The national screening programme invites women for breast checks.

items.definitionEn: finding a disease at a stage when treatment works better
items.example: Early detection of cancer can mean less aggressive surgery.

items.definitionEn: an illness that vaccination, hygiene or lifestyle change can stop
items.example: Measles is a preventable disease, yet outbreaks still occur.

items.definitionEn: a system in which everyone can get medical care, usually paid from taxes
items.example: Supporters of universal healthcare argue that no one should face ruinous bills.

items.definitionEn: medical care paid for by the patient or a private insurer, not the state
items.example: Some families buy private healthcare to avoid long waiting lists.

items.definitionEn: moral rules that guide doctors, such as doing no harm and respecting choice
items.example: Medical ethics forbids forcing treatment on a competent adult.

items.definitionEn: agreement to treatment after the risks and benefits have been explained
items.example: Surgery cannot start without informed consent, except in a true emergency.

items.definitionEn: the duty to keep a patient’s medical information private
items.example: Patient confidentiality means results are not discussed in a public corridor.

items.definitionEn: a disease that lasts a long time and often cannot be fully cured
items.example: A chronic illness such as asthma needs a long-term treatment plan.

items.definitionEn: an illness that starts suddenly and is often severe but may be short
items.example: An acute illness can still put a healthy adult in hospital overnight.

items.definitionEn: an illness caused by bacteria, viruses or other microbes that can spread
items.example: Hand-washing remains a cheap defence against infectious disease.

items.definitionEn: a long-term illness that is not passed from person to person, such as diabetes
items.example: Diet and exercise influence many types of non-communicable disease.

items.definitionEn: able to spread from one person to another
items.example: Stay at home while the infection is still contagious.

items.definitionEn: a sudden rise in cases of a disease in a place or group
items.example: The school closed after an outbreak of norovirus.

items.definitionEn: when a disease spreads quickly to many people in a region
items.example: An influenza epidemic filled hospital wards in January.

items.definitionEn: an epidemic that spreads across many countries or the whole world
items.example: A pandemic tests both hospitals and the supply of medicines.

items.definitionEn: the body’s ability to resist a particular infection
items.example: Previous infection does not always give lasting immunity.

items.definitionEn: protection that appears when enough people in a group are immune
items.example: Herd immunity is harder to reach if vaccination rates fall.

items.definitionEn: a protein the body makes to recognise and fight a specific germ
items.example: A blood test can show whether you have an antibody after vaccination.

items.definitionEn: giving a vaccine to protect someone from a disease
items.example: Childhood vaccination has almost wiped out some dangerous infections.

items.definitionEn: an extra vaccine given later to strengthen protection
items.example: Older adults were offered a booster dose before winter.

items.definitionEn: delay or refusal of a vaccine despite it being available
items.example: Clear information can reduce vaccine hesitancy more than pressure.

items.definitionEn: the process of becoming protected against a disease, usually by vaccine
items.example: The immunisation schedule is published by the health ministry.

items.definitionEn: keeping people who may be infected away from others for a set time
items.example: Travellers from the affected region had to quarantine for ten days.

items.definitionEn: staying at home and away from others because you are ill or at risk
items.example: Self-isolation is pointless if you still go to the supermarket.

items.definitionEn: the body’s painful, red or swollen reaction to injury or infection
items.example: Chronic inflammation in the joints makes walking difficult.

items.definitionEn: an illness in which the immune system attacks the body’s own tissue
items.example: An autoimmune disease may need lifelong medicine, not a short course of antibiotics.

items.definitionEn: illness of the heart and blood vessels
items.example: Cardiovascular disease remains a leading cause of death in Europe.

items.definitionEn: illness of the lungs and airways
items.example: Air pollution worsens respiratory disease in cities.

items.definitionEn: a sudden blockage of blood to part of the heart muscle
items.example: Chest pain that spreads to the arm can be a heart attack — call 112.

items.definitionEn: a sudden loss of brain function because blood supply is blocked or a vessel bursts
items.example: Fast treatment after a stroke can limit lasting damage.

items.definitionEn: blood pressure that stays too high and damages organs over time
items.example: Hypertension often has no obvious symptoms until a crisis.

items.definitionEn: a long-term condition in which the body cannot use insulin properly
items.example: Type 2 diabetes can often be delayed by diet and activity.

items.definitionEn: an abnormal lump of cells that may be benign or malignant
items.example: The scan showed a tumour that had not yet spread.

items.definitionEn: medical care such as surgery, drugs or radiotherapy used against cancer
items.example: Cancer treatment can last months and still allow some people to work.

items.definitionEn: a disease that cannot be cured and will lead to death
items.example: Hospice staff support families facing a terminal illness.

items.definitionEn: a period when signs of a disease have reduced or disappeared
items.example: She has been in remission for three years after chemotherapy.

items.definitionEn: the return of an illness after a period of improvement
items.example: A relapse does not mean that all previous progress was wasted.

items.definitionEn: an extra medical problem that appears because of a disease or treatment
items.example: Infection is a possible complication after surgery.

items.definitionEn: a doctor’s judgement of how an illness is likely to develop
items.example: The prognosis is better when the disease is found early.

items.definitionEn: the identification of an illness after tests and examination
items.example: A delayed diagnosis can make later treatment harder.

items.definitionEn: a crack or break in a bone
items.example: The X-ray confirmed a fracture of the wrist.

items.definitionEn: damage to the brain caused by a blow, jolt or penetrating wound
items.example: A traumatic brain injury can change memory and mood for months.

items.definitionEn: pain that lasts for months and often needs a mix of treatments
items.example: Chronic pain is not always visible, which can make stigma worse.

items.definitionEn: an illness caused by conditions at work, such as dust or chemicals
items.example: Hearing loss can be an occupational disease in noisy factories.

items.definitionEn: a sudden, life-threatening allergic reaction
items.example: Anaphylaxis needs adrenaline at once, then emergency care.

items.definitionEn: when bacteria survive drugs that used to kill them
items.example: Antibiotic resistance grows if people take leftover tablets “just in case”.

items.definitionEn: an infection passed through sexual contact
items.example: A sexually transmitted infection can be present without clear symptoms.

items.definitionEn: a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing
items.example: An antibiotic will not help a typical viral cold.

items.definitionEn: a written order from a doctor for a medicine
items.example: Take this prescription to the chemist the same day.

items.definitionEn: a medicine with the same active ingredient as a brand-name product, usually cheaper
items.example: The pharmacist offered a generic drug at half the price.

items.definitionEn: a drug you can buy without a doctor’s order
items.example: Ask the pharmacist before mixing any over-the-counter medicine with alcohol.

items.definitionEn: the amount of a medicine that should be taken at one time
items.example: Never exceed the recommended dose printed on the packet.

items.definitionEn: an unwanted result of a medicine or treatment
items.example: Drowsiness is a common side effect of this antihistamine.

items.definitionEn: a carefully controlled test of a new treatment in people
items.example: Volunteers in a clinical trial are told the risks in writing.

items.definitionEn: a dummy treatment with no active drug, used to test whether a medicine really works
items.example: Half the group received a placebo so the results could be compared fairly.

items.definitionEn: a medical operation that involves cutting or repairing the body
items.example: He will need surgery on his knee before he can walk unaided.

items.definitionEn: an operation done through small cuts, often with a camera
items.example: Keyhole surgery usually means a shorter stay in hospital.

items.definitionEn: an operation that replaces a failing organ with one from a donor
items.example: An organ transplant requires lifelong medicine to prevent rejection.

items.definitionEn: a person who gives an organ for transplant, in life or after death
items.example: Carrying a card shows you wish to be an organ donor.

items.definitionEn: putting donated blood into a patient’s vein
items.example: A blood transfusion was needed after the accident.

items.definitionEn: treatment that uses movement, exercise and massage to restore function
items.example: Physiotherapy after the fracture helped her climb stairs again.

items.definitionEn: treatment that helps people manage daily tasks after illness or disability
items.example: Occupational therapy taught him new ways to dress with one hand.

items.definitionEn: treatments outside standard scientific medicine, such as some herbal or needle therapies
items.example: Alternative medicine should not replace a treatment your specialist has prescribed.

items.definitionEn: a therapy that uses thin needles at specific points on the body
items.example: Some patients try acupuncture for long-term back pain.

items.definitionEn: a programme of therapy to regain strength or skills after illness or injury
items.example: Medical rehabilitation after a stroke can take many months of daily practice.

items.definitionEn: care that relieves pain and stress when a disease cannot be cured
items.example: Palliative care can start long before the last weeks of life.

items.definitionEn: a place or service that cares for people with a terminal illness
items.example: The hospice offered overnight rooms for relatives.

items.definitionEn: planned medical help to reduce long-term or severe pain
items.example: Pain management may combine physiotherapy, medicine and counselling.

items.definitionEn: an agreed set of steps for how a patient will be treated
items.example: The treatment plan was explained to the family in plain language.

items.definitionEn: a later visit to check how treatment is working
items.example: Book a follow-up appointment two weeks after the procedure.

items.definitionEn: a record of past illnesses, operations, allergies and medicines
items.example: Always mention allergies when you give your medical history.

items.definitionEn: a drug that stops you feeling pain during a procedure
items.example: A local anaesthetic numbs the area but you stay awake.

items.definitionEn: a detailed image of the inside of the body made with magnets, not X-rays
items.example: The MRI scan showed a small tear in the cartilage.

items.definitionEn: the hospital room where surgeons perform operations
items.example: She was taken to the operating theatre at seven in the morning.

items.definitionEn: removal of a small piece of tissue so it can be tested
items.example: The biopsy confirmed that the lump was benign.

items.definitionEn: a general doctor you visit first, not a hospital specialist
items.example: Phone your GP if the fever lasts more than three days.

items.definitionEn: the United Kingdom’s publicly funded health service
items.example: Treatment on the NHS is generally free at the point of use.

items.definitionEn: the hospital department for sudden serious illness or injury
items.example: Go to A&E if the bleeding does not stop or you cannot breathe.

items.definitionEn: a list of patients who must wait for a test, operation or specialist
items.example: The waiting list for a hip replacement is still over a year.

items.definitionEn: a policy that pays some or all of your medical costs
items.example: Health insurance may not cover dental work or physiotherapy.

items.definitionEn: the clinic where a general practitioner sees patients
items.example: The GP surgery opens at eight and closes at six on weekdays.

items.definitionEn: a written request from a GP for you to see a specialist
items.example: You need a referral before the hospital will book the scan.

items.definitionEn: a senior hospital specialist who leads a patient’s hospital care
items.example: The consultant explained the risks of the operation in person.

items.definitionEn: a patient who visits hospital for treatment but does not stay overnight
items.example: Most chemotherapy is given on an outpatient basis.

items.definitionEn: a patient who stays in hospital overnight or longer
items.example: As an inpatient you will be on the surgical ward.

items.definitionEn: official permission to leave hospital after treatment
items.example: Discharge was delayed until a carer could be arranged at home.

items.definitionEn: the written or digital file of a patient’s history and treatment
items.example: You have the right to see your own medical records.

items.definitionEn: advice from another doctor about a diagnosis or treatment
items.example: Families often seek a second opinion before major surgery.

items.definitionEn: the organised network of hospitals, clinics, staff and funding in a country
items.example: An ageing population puts pressure on every healthcare system.

items.definitionEn: first-contact health services, especially GPs, dentists and pharmacies
items.example: Strong primary care keeps minor problems out of hospital.

items.definitionEn: hospital and specialist services after a GP referral
items.example: Secondary care includes surgery, scans and most consultant clinics.

items.definitionEn: a trained emergency clinician who treats people at the scene and in an ambulance
items.example: The paramedic started treatment before they reached A&E.

items.definitionEn: a specialist who cares for women during pregnancy, birth and after
items.example: The midwife visited the family at home on the third day.

items.definitionEn: a doctor who specialises in the health of babies and children
items.example: The paediatrician adjusted the dose for the child’s weight.

items.definitionEn: a doctor who gives anaesthetics and watches the patient during surgery
items.example: The anaesthetist asked about previous reactions to drugs.

items.definitionEn: a professional who prepares and advises on medicines
items.example: Ask the pharmacist if two medicines are safe to take together.

items.definitionEn: medical consultation by phone or video instead of a face-to-face visit
items.example: Telemedicine helped rural patients speak to a specialist without travel.

items.definitionEn: a clinic you can attend without booking in advance
items.example: The walk-in centre treated the cut and sent her home the same morning.

items.definitionEn: medical help available when the usual GP surgery is closed
items.example: Call the out-of-hours service rather than waiting until Monday.

items.definitionEn: harm caused when care falls below the standard a patient should expect
items.example: A claim for medical negligence can take years to resolve.

items.definitionEn: the condition of your mind and emotions, including how you cope with life
items.example: Schools now treat mental health as seriously as physical fitness.

items.definitionEn: a mental-health condition with intense, lasting worry that disrupts daily life
items.example: An anxiety disorder is not the same as ordinary exam nerves.

items.definitionEn: talking regularly with a trained person to work through emotional problems
items.example: She started counselling after months of panic on the way to school.

items.definitionEn: unfair shame or discrimination attached to an illness or situation
items.example: Stigma still stops many men from asking for psychological help.

items.definitionEn: a mental illness with lasting low mood, loss of interest and often poor sleep
items.example: Depression is an illness, not a sign of weakness or laziness.

items.definitionEn: a condition with extreme swings between high and low mood
items.example: Bipolar disorder needs specialist care, not advice to “cheer up”.

items.definitionEn: an eating disorder involving severe food restriction and a distorted body image
items.example: Anorexia nervosa can affect boys as well as girls and needs specialist care.

items.definitionEn: a condition after a shocking event, with flashbacks, nightmares and high alertness
items.example: Post-traumatic stress disorder can appear months after an accident.

items.definitionEn: a state of feeling drained and unable to cope after prolonged stress
items.example: Emotional exhaustion is more than a busy week — it needs rest and a change of load.

items.definitionEn: treatment that uses structured conversation rather than only medicine
items.example: Talking therapy can work alongside antidepressants.

items.definitionEn: a talking treatment that helps people change unhelpful thoughts and habits
items.example: Cognitive behavioural therapy is widely used for anxiety and depression.

items.definitionEn: a medical doctor who diagnoses mental illness and can prescribe medicine
items.example: A psychiatrist reviewed the dose after the first month.

items.definitionEn: a specialist in behaviour and the mind who offers assessment and therapy but is not a medical doctor
items.example: The psychologist used tests as well as interviews.

items.definitionEn: a trained person who listens and helps you talk through problems
items.example: The school counsellor keeps meetings confidential unless you are in danger.

items.definitionEn: a sudden episode of intense fear with physical symptoms such as a racing heart
items.example: A panic attack is frightening but it is not a heart attack.

items.definitionEn: a lasting difficulty falling or staying asleep
items.example: Caffeine late in the day can worsen insomnia.

items.definitionEn: a method you use to manage stress or difficult emotions
items.example: Exercise can be a healthy coping strategy if it does not become compulsive.

items.definitionEn: people with a similar problem who meet to share experience and encouragement
items.example: The support group meets every Thursday in the community centre.

items.definitionEn: hurting yourself on purpose as a way of dealing with emotional pain
items.example: Teachers must take self-harm seriously and seek professional support.

items.definitionEn: a point when a person cannot stay safe or cope and needs urgent help
items.example: A mental-health crisis line is not a substitute for long-term therapy, but it can keep someone safe overnight.

items.definitionEn: a condition in which you cannot control a harmful habit even when you want to stop
items.example: Addiction changes the brain, which is why willpower alone often fails.

items.definitionEn: harmful or risky use of alcohol, drugs or other substances
items.example: Substance abuse in the family affects children even if they do not drink.

items.definitionEn: addiction to alcohol that damages health, work or relationships
items.example: Alcoholism is a medical condition, not a moral failure.

items.definitionEn: physical and psychological dependence on nicotine from tobacco or vapes
items.example: Nicotine addiction can start after only a few weeks of regular vaping.

items.definitionEn: unpleasant physical or mental effects when a dependent person stops a substance
items.example: Withdrawal symptoms are a reason to seek medical help, not to give up quitting.

items.definitionEn: policies that lower the damage of drug use even if the person is not yet abstinent
items.example: Needle programmes are an example of harm reduction, not an invitation to start.

items.definitionEn: drinking a large amount of alcohol in a short time
items.example: Binge drinking at weekends still damages the liver over the years.

items.definitionEn: breathing in other people’s tobacco smoke
items.example: Passive smoking raises the risk of asthma in children.

items.definitionEn: inhaling vapour from an electronic cigarette
items.example: Vaping is not harmless, even if it is often less toxic than cigarettes.

items.definitionEn: an inability to control betting despite serious harm
items.example: Gambling addiction can destroy a family’s finances in months.

items.definitionEn: a centre that treats people for addiction, often with therapy and medical support
items.example: He spent six weeks in a rehab clinic after leaving hospital.

items.definitionEn: a drug or chemical that can create dependence
items.example: An addictive substance may be legal, like alcohol, or banned.

items.definitionEn: habits such as balanced eating, activity, sleep and avoiding harmful substances
items.example: A healthy lifestyle lowers the risk of several long-term diseases.

items.definitionEn: a way of living with little physical movement
items.example: A sedentary lifestyle is linked to type 2 diabetes and back pain.

items.definitionEn: a level of body fat in children that is high enough to harm present and future health
items.example: Childhood obesity has become a public-health priority in many countries.

items.definitionEn: poor health caused by too little food, or food that lacks essential nutrients
items.example: Undernutrition can occur in hospitals if patients cannot eat enough.

items.definitionEn: a lasting lack of enough sleep
items.example: Sleep deprivation harms concentration as much as a small amount of alcohol.

items.definitionEn: paying attention to the present moment, often used to reduce stress
items.example: Ten minutes of mindfulness is not a cure, but it can calm racing thoughts.

items.definitionEn: not doing enough movement to protect health
items.example: Physical inactivity is a separate risk from being overweight.

items.definitionEn: a physical, sensory, intellectual or mental condition that makes some activities harder
items.example: Disability is not only a medical fact — barriers in buildings matter too.

items.definitionEn: how easily people with disabilities can use a place, service or product
items.example: Accessibility includes ramps, captions and clear signs, not only a wheelchair icon.

items.definitionEn: a practical change an employer or school must make so a disabled person can take part
items.example: A reasonable adjustment might be extra time in an exam or a ground-floor classroom.

items.definitionEn: the possibility for a wheelchair user to enter and move around a place
items.example: Wheelchair access at the station still requires a member of staff with a ramp.

items.definitionEn: a visual language using hands, face and body, used by many deaf people
items.example: Public events should offer a sign language interpreter, not only a microphone.

items.definitionEn: having little or no sight
items.example: A visually impaired passenger may need an announcement, not only a screen.

items.definitionEn: partial or complete loss of hearing
items.example: A hearing impairment is not the same as being unwilling to listen.

items.definitionEn: a reduced ability to understand new or complex information and to learn new skills
items.example: Adults with a learning disability still have the right to make choices about their care.

items.definitionEn: the idea that brains differ and that autism, ADHD and similar conditions are variations, not only defects
items.example: Neurodiversity in the classroom needs quieter rooms as well as extra time.

items.definitionEn: a device such as a stick, frame or wheelchair that helps a person move
items.example: A mobility aid should be fitted by a specialist, not bought at random online.

items.definitionEn: a trained dog that helps a blind or visually impaired person travel safely
items.example: A guide dog is a working animal, not a pet you should stroke without asking.

items.definitionEn: a system of raised dots that blind people read by touch
items.example: Lift buttons should include Braille as well as large print.

items.definitionPl: opiekun osoby chorej lub z niepełnosprawnością
items.definitionEn: a person who looks after someone ill, elderly or disabled, often unpaid
items.example: A young carer may miss school if no respite is offered.

items.definitionEn: ongoing help with daily life for people who cannot live fully independently
items.example: Long-term care is expensive, whether it is at home or in a home.

items.definitionEn: a route into a building or vehicle that does not require climbing steps
items.example: Step-free access at every platform is still a distant goal on many railways.

items.definitionEn: simple medical help given before professional care arrives
items.example: Every workplace should have staff trained in first aid.

items.definitionEn: lying someone on their side so the airway stays open if they are unconscious but breathing
items.example: Put an unconscious breathing person in the recovery position and call 112.

items.definitionEn: chest compressions, and sometimes rescue breaths, to keep blood moving when the heart has stopped
items.example: Early CPR doubles the chance of survival after cardiac arrest.

items.definitionEn: a device that can restart the heart with a controlled electric shock
items.example: A public defibrillator on the wall is useless if nobody knows the code.

items.definitionEn: inward and upward presses on the upper abdomen to clear a blocked airway
items.example: Abdominal thrusts are used when a person is choking and cannot cough or speak.

items.definitionEn: sorting patients so the most urgent cases are treated first
items.example: Triage at A&E explains why a broken arm may wait while chest pain goes in first.

items.definitionPl: nagły stan zagrożenia życia lub zdrowia
items.definitionEn: a sudden, serious health event that needs immediate professional help
items.example: Difficulty breathing is a medical emergency, not something to sleep off.

items.definitionEn: organisations such as ambulance, fire and police that respond to urgent incidents
items.example: Give a clear address when you call the emergency services.

items.definitionEn: a device a person at risk of anaphylaxis can use to inject adrenaline quickly
items.example: Keep the adrenaline auto-injector with you, not in a locker downstairs.

items.definitionEn: giving your blood so it can be used for patients who need it
items.example: Regular blood donation is one of the simplest ways to save lives.

items.definitionEn: a document showing you agree that your organs may be used after death
items.example: A donor card should be backed up by telling your family your wishes.

items.definitionEn: intentionally ending a person’s life to relieve suffering from a terminal illness, illegal in many countries
items.example: Euthanasia is a frequent topic in Matura essays on medical ethics.

items.definitionEn: an official note from a doctor confirming illness or fitness
items.example: The employer asked for a medical certificate after the third day off.

items.definitionEn: basic measurements such as pulse, temperature, breathing rate and blood pressure
items.example: Nurses record vital signs several times a day on the ward.
